I am seventy years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou since I was a young man. My bones ache more than they used to, and I cannot bend and lift like I once did, but my eyes still know when the wheat is thirsty and my hands still remember the feel of good soil. I only finished primary school, but fifty years of watching the seasons turn has taught me more than any book.

This year, I will stick to what I know: the winter wheat and summer maize rotation on my six mu of flat, irrigated land. I thought about cotton, but at my age I do not have the strength for the endless picking. Vegetables fetch a good price at the market, but the buyers cheat you and the prices jump around. Wheat and maize are safe. The grain station takes them, my family eats them, and I can hire the combine for both harvests.

For the wheat, I will sow in early October after rotary tillage. I will use the improved *shimai* seed at about thirty jin per mu—my neighbor saved some for me, but I will buy fresh seed for two mu to be safe. I will put down a basal compound fertilizer and irrigate four times: once before winter to protect the seedlings from the cold, and three more times in spring when the wheat starts to joint and fill. I will spray for insects twice, put down herbicide once, and use fungicide once when the weather turns humid. If all goes well, I expect about one thousand jin per mu.

As soon as the wheat comes off in early June, I will plant the summer maize directly into the stubble without tillage—there is no time to waste, and the no-tillage seeder saves my back. I will use a hybrid variety like *nongda372*; one small package per mu is enough. Maize needs less fuss than wheat: two irrigations, usually one right after sowing and one at the tasseling stage. I will spray insecticide twice and herbicide once. With good rain, I should get about eleven hundred jin per mu.

I do not chase the highest yields anymore. I aim for steady, sure harvests that will feed my family and leave a little grain to sell.

The winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping system is the only sensible choice: it is reliable, mechanized, and matches the local climate and water availability. I use improved wheat seed with rotary tillage and four irrigations, and hybrid maize planted no-till immediately after the wheat harvest with two irrigations.
